name: Falcon Heavy
summary: Three Falcon 9-derived cores side by side, 70 m tall and 12.2 m wide, with 27 Merlin engines. This shows a flight like its second launch (Arabsat-6A, April 2019), when both side boosters flew back and landed.

info.summary: The middle booster: a strengthened Falcon 9 first stage that carries the second stage and payload.
info.purpose: Throttles down early on to save propellant, so it keeps burning for about a minute after the side boosters separate.
info.funFact: Because it flies faster and farther than the side boosters, the centre core can't fly home. It lands on a drone ship far out at sea instead, or is expended.

info.summary: Nine Merlin 1D engines: eight in a ring around a centre engine, in a structure called the octaweb.
info.purpose: Burn RP-1 kerosene with liquid oxygen. Some can be relit several times, which is what makes landing possible: three for the boostback and entry burns, one for the landing burn.
info.funFact: The engines are throttleable. Even so, one Merlin at its lowest setting is more than the near-empty booster weighs, so it can't hover. The landing burn has to reach zero speed exactly at the ground.

info.summary: The lower tank, holding RP-1 kerosene.
info.purpose: Feeds fuel to the Merlins. On a landing flight, some of it is held back for the return burns.

info.summary: The upper tank, holding liquid oxygen chilled below its normal boiling point so more fits in.
info.purpose: Supplies the oxidizer. Chilling the propellants makes them denser, so the tanks hold more.

info.summary: The black composite section at the top of the booster.
info.purpose: Joins the two stages, covers the second stage's engine nozzle, and carries the grid fins and the pneumatic pushers that separate the stages.

info.summary: Four folding legs, stowed flat against the booster during launch.
info.purpose: Swing down a few seconds before touchdown and absorb the landing.

info.summary: One of the four landing legs (east side).
info.purpose: Hinged at its foot: a pneumatic system swings it down and out just before touchdown.

info.purpose: Hinged at its foot: a pneumatic system swings it down and out just before touchdown.

info.summary: Four lattice-shaped fins near the top of the booster, folded up during launch.
info.purpose: Unfold after separation and steer the booster as it falls back through the atmosphere, a bit like the flaps on a plane.
info.funFact: Grid fins work even when the booster is falling backwards at supersonic speed, which ordinary flat fins struggle with.

info.summary: One of the four titanium grid fins (east side).
info.purpose: Each fin swivels independently to steer the falling booster.

info.summary: The left side booster: essentially a Falcon 9 first stage with a nose cone, strapped to the centre core.
info.purpose: Together with the centre core, the two side boosters give 27 engines at liftoff. They burn out first, separate and fly back to land at Cape Canaveral.
info.funFact: On Falcon Heavy's first two flights, the two side boosters landed side by side, seconds apart, at Landing Zones 1 and 2.

info.summary: The same upper stage Falcon 9 uses: one Merlin Vacuum engine.
info.purpose: Lights after the centre core separates and carries the payload to orbit. It can restart, as it does later in this mission to reach a high transfer orbit.

info.summary: A Merlin with a large nozzle extension for vacuum.
info.purpose: In vacuum, a bigger nozzle gets more push out of the same exhaust.

info.summary: RP-1 and liquid-oxygen tanks.
info.purpose: Built on the same tooling as the boosters.

info.summary: The satellite and its fairing.
info.purpose: With 27 engines at liftoff, Falcon Heavy can carry about 63.8 tonnes to low Earth orbit, though recovered boosters reduce that.

info.summary: Half of the 5.2 m fairing, the same one Falcon 9 uses.
info.purpose: Protects the satellite through the atmosphere, then splits away.
materials: Carbon fibre over an aluminium honeycomb core

info.summary: A large communications satellite, like Arabsat-6A, which weighed about 6.5 tonnes.
info.purpose: Bound for a high transfer orbit; the second stage relights later to get it there.

events.title: Countdown
events.caption: Three cores and 27 Merlin engines are fuelled. The engines ignite in a staggered sequence just before liftoff.

events.title: Liftoff
events.caption: Liftoff with about 22,800 kN of thrust from 27 engines, more than any other rocket flying at the time of its first launch in 2018.

events.title: Max-Q
events.caption: Maximum aerodynamic pressure. The centre core has been throttled down to save propellant for later.

events.title: Side boosters cut off
events.caption: BECO: the two side boosters shut down, about two and a half minutes into the flight.

events.title: Side booster separation
events.caption: The side boosters separate and peel away to either side, then begin their trip back to Cape Canaveral.

events.title: Side boosters: boostback
events.caption: The camera follows the left side booster. Both boosters flip around and relight three engines to head back towards land, flying in formation.

events.title: Centre core cutoff
events.caption: High above, the centre core's engines shut down at T+3:31. Four seconds later it separates, and the second stage lights at T+3:42.

events.title: Fairing jettison (on the second stage)
events.caption: The second stage drops its fairing at T+4:07. Below, the side boosters coast to the top of their arc.

events.title: Side boosters: entry burn
events.caption: Both boosters relight to slow down as they fall back into thicker air.

events.title: Side boosters: landing burn
events.caption: Each booster's centre engine lights for the final braking burn.

events.title: Legs deploy
events.caption: Landing legs swing down on both boosters.

events.title: Double touchdown
events.caption: At T+7:51 the side boosters touch down at Landing Zones 1 and 2, seconds apart, with twin sonic booms across the Space Coast.

events.title: Back to the second stage
events.caption: The second stage is still burning towards its parking orbit. The centre core will land on a drone ship at sea at about T+9:48.

events.title: SECO 1
events.caption: Second engine cutoff at T+8:48: parking orbit. The second stage will relight about 19 minutes later to send the satellite towards geostationary orbit.
